title: Majestic
reviewNotes: All 53 accepted source images and captions re-reviewed. Native images 47–51 establish bxc4/bxc4 and the final pawn race. The complete seven-piece start after ...b3 is a disclosed one-ply bridge across the 132–133 second samples: the preceding Black-to-move diagram has exactly one legal move, ...b3. Three branches check the source c5/b2/c6/b1=Q/c7 mate, an independent knight-underpromotion defense, and the losing Kd6 king release. Earlier eleven-piece rook/knight sacrifices remain unverified source context.
transcript: White's brilliant idea is king to e7, sacrificing the white rook completely. But of course, taking the rook would be a blunder because rook to c4 would be a checkmate. But black doesn't have to take the white rook. He can hit white with a counter brilliancy. Now sacrificing the black knight because after the knight is taken, the rook is going to fly to h7, maintaining the attack on the white rook and preparing a skewer. And if white tries to save the material with rook to d8, after this check, the king will have to move. And actually black cannot win the white rook. This would allow white to push the king in the corner and win the black rook. But what black can do is just repeat moves and force a draw by repetition. But white does have a more resilient way to play the beautiful rook a8. This move still loses the rook to the skewer, but on white's terms because now after this check, the black king is forced to run to the corner and banish his own rook [music] to the edge of the board. But this shouldn't bother black. He's just going to be able to play h6, move the king, and then free up the rook, which is exactly the reason why white plays a6, preventing that idea. But the brilliant mind of the player with the black pieces has not run out of resources, and he plays pawn to b5, now attacking the rook and setting up a sneaky trap. If the white rook moves anywhere on this rank, the black king is going to be able to break free from the bind and you cannot check him anymore, which means that the black rook will run free. But if instead of that, the white rook goes anywhere on this file, this is actually going to be a surprising stalemate. Black has no legal moves, but is not checkmated, so this is a draw. So is this it? Is black simply out of the woods in this position? Well, not exactly. White had actually foreseen all of this, and he has one last majestic move, the incredible king 2d7. Leaving the rook to hang, and that is actually the only legal move of black. And this of course doesn't seem [music] to make any sense. White is now only left with two pawns against two pawns and a rook. And not only that, black is going to get a queen way faster than white. But you see, despite the material imbalance, it's the position to win the game. Because pawn 2 c7 is a beautiful checkmate. [music]
